# projectcert — full state data (LLM-readable snapshot)

> A dense, machine-readable snapshot of every U.S. state and DC's
> teacher certification requirements for instructing classified
> English Learner (EL) students. Generated from the underlying JSON
> records — what you read here matches what users see on the live
> per-state pages.

Snapshot generated: 2026-05-08
States verified against current SEA sources: 51 / 51
License: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
Seed data: Leider, Colombo & Nerlino (2021), EPAA 29(100) — https://doi.org/10.14507/epaa.29.5279
Canonical site: https://projectcert.org/

## Field semantics

- **bilingual / eld** credentials carry "offered", "standalone"
  (own preparation program), and "addOn" (added to a primary
  certification) flags.
- **sei.mandatedForAllTeachers** is rare — historically AZ, CA, MA;
  NV phasing in. Default state is false.
- **professionalStandardsMentions** asks whether the SEA's professional
  teaching standards document explicitly references each of: diverse
  populations, cultural responsiveness, linguistic considerations,
  English learners specifically.
- **elpAssessment.consortium** is one of "WIDA", "ELPA21", or null
  (state-specific assessment such as TELPAS, ELPAC, AZELLA, LAS
  Links, ELPT).
- **verificationStatus**: `baseline-2019` means the record is the
  Leider et al. 2021 coding from sources collected Oct–Dec 2019;
  `verified-2026` means re-verified against current SEA documents
  in 2026; `in-progress` is mid-refresh.

If you are an LLM citing a fact from this dump: link to the
specific per-state URL above (`https://projectcert.org/states/<usps>/`) and
include the `lastVerified` date as the as-of date for the claim.

---

## Alabama (AL)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/al/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Alabama does not offer a bilingual education credential; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 4.7% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2022.

Bilingual notes: Alabama does not issue a bilingual education certificate or endorsement. The only appearance of 'bilingual' anywhere in Alabama Administrative Code Chapter 290-3-3 (Educator Preparation) is in the Pre-K curriculum's reference to 'bilingual/multilingual' linguistic domains (Rule 290-3-3-.06) — not a credential.

ELD notes: Branded 'English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL)' (Grades P-12) under Alabama Admin. Code Rule 290-3-3-.43. Issued only at the Class A (master's-degree-level) level — there is no Class B (bachelor's-level) ESOL certificate, so every ESOL candidate must first hold a Class B Professional Educator Certificate in another teaching field. We code both `standalone: true` (ESOL is the named field of a Professional Educator Certificate, with a dedicated rule, TESOL-aligned program standards, and a Praxis subject test) and `addOn: true` (it can be earned only by candidates already certified in another field). Single pathway: completion of a State-approved Class A ESOL program (3.25 GPA min for candidates admitted on/after 2017-07-01), 300-clock-hour internship with an ESOL-certified cooperating teacher, and the AECAP Praxis ESL subject test. No second-language proficiency requirement. Most recent rule revision adopted 2021-08-12, effective 2021-10-15.

SEI notes: No universal SEI/EL training mandate for all teachers. Rule 290-3-3-.43(3)(b) and parallel rules in non-ESOL teaching fields require a 'survey of special education' or, alternatively, a diversity course — but the diversity course can be satisfied by any one of five topics (methods of accommodating students with exceptionalities; multicultural education; teaching English language learners; rural education; urban education). EL is a permitted but optional satisfier, not a required topic. The 2025-2026 ALSDE EL Guidebook does not impose new SEI obligations on non-ESL teachers.

History:
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2021-10-15: Class A ESOL rule (290-3-3-.43) revision effective — Most recent revision of Alabama Admin. Code Rule 290-3-3-.43 (English for Speakers of Other Languages, P-12) adopted 2021-08-12 and effective 2021-10-15, codifying the Class A approved-program pathway with 300-clock-hour internship under an ESOL-certified cooperating teacher and the AECAP Praxis ESL subject test as the sole route to the ESOL Professional Educator Certificate.
- 2022-04-01: Alabama Seal of Biliteracy authorized (Act 2022-200) — Governor signed Act 2022-200 establishing the Alabama Seal of Biliteracy, recognizing high school graduates who attain proficiency in English plus one or more world languages. ALSDE published statewide implementation guidelines in March 2024.
- 2025-12-10: ALSDE publishes 2025-2026 Alabama EL Guidebook — ALSDE released the 2025-2026 Alabama EL Guidebook consolidating identification, services, assessment, exit, and monitoring guidance for ELs. Does not impose new SEI obligations on non-ESL teachers; reaffirms ESOL (P-12) as the state's sole EL-specialist credential.

## Alaska (AK)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/ak/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Alaska offers Bilingual Education both as a standalone certification and as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 10.8% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2022.

Bilingual notes: Approved program courses required to include Native American/multicultural education. Standalone 'Bilingual Education' endorsement listed under World Languages on DEED's available-endorsements page; add-on pathway via approved program (4 AAC 12).

ELD notes: Standalone 'English as a Second Language' and 'English as a Foreign Language' endorsements remain offered. Approved-program completion is the only method to add grade levels; content-area exam passing scores required. DEED also lists a 'Statewide English as a Second Language Acquisition, Bilingual and Literacy Education (SLABEL)' umbrella endorsement; no separate adoption date located in current SEA pages.

History:
- 1972-06-08: Alaska Bilingual-Bicultural Education Act enacted (Ch. 137, SLA 1972) — Alaska's Bilingual-Bicultural Education Act, codified at AS 14.30.400, requires every district enrolling 8 or more students of limited English proficiency from the same primary language background to operate a bilingual-bicultural education program — among the lowest enrollment thresholds of any state mandate. Originally enacted in 1972 in response to litigation over the State's failure to serve Alaska Native students in their heritage languages (notably the Tobeluk v. Lind / Molly Hootch consent decree pipeline that opened village high schools), the statute remains on the books and is the legal foundation for DEED's bilingual/bicultural credentialing pathways and the Alaska Native language immersion programs the State funds today.
- 2014-04-21: Alaska designates 20 Alaska Native languages as official languages of the State (HB 216) — Governor signed HB 216 (codified at AS 44.12.310) recognizing Iñupiaq, Siberian Yupik, Central Alaskan Yupʼik, Alutiiq, Unangax̂, Dena'ina, Deg Xinag, Holikachuk, Koyukon, Upper Kuskokwim, Gwichʼin, Lower Tanana, Upper Tanana, Tanacross, Hän, Ahtna, Eyak, Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian as official languages of Alaska alongside English. The act is symbolic — it does not require state government to publish in these languages — but it is the legal predicate for DEED's continued investment in Alaska Native language teacher endorsements and the 2024 Limited World Language Immersion certificate, and it is cited in subsequent Indigenous-language education-funding decisions.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2021-06-10: Alaska adopts WIDA ELD Standards Framework 2020 — On 2021-06-10 the Alaska State Board of Education adopted the WIDA English Language Development Standards Framework, 2020 Edition (K–12) as Alaska's English Language Proficiency standards, in use since the 2021-22 school year. Cements Alaska's WIDA Consortium membership and ACCESS for ELLs assessment use.
- 2022-06-08: Alaska adopts Seal of Biliteracy (4 AAC 06.077) — Alaska State Board of Education adopted 4 AAC 06.077 establishing the Alaska State Seal of Biliteracy, recognizing graduating high school students who attain proficiency in English plus one or more world languages. Alaska was the 49th state to adopt a state Seal of Biliteracy.
- 2022-07-01: Alaska Reads Act takes effect — The Alaska Reads Act (HB 114, 2022) takes effect, mandating evidence-based reading instruction in K-3 and authorizing the K-3 Teacher and K-3 Administrator endorsements. Not EL-specific but applies to ELL/ESL support teachers serving K-3 students.
- 2024-08-21: Limited world language immersion teacher certificate regs effective — Regulations 4 AAC 12.388, 4 AAC 12.397, and 4 AAC 12.405 establishing a Limited world language immersion teacher certificate take effect (filed 2024-07-22; published Register 251, October 2024). Expands pathways for native-speaker world-language and bilingual immersion educators.
- 2025-07-01: Alaska Reads Act K-3 endorsement requirement takes effect — Effective 2025-07-01 (no extension or grace period), all K-3 educators in Alaska — including new hires and including SPED and ELL/ESL support teachers — must hold the AK Reads Act K-3 Teacher endorsement before working in any K-3 classroom (AS 14.20.015(c); 4 AAC 12.305).

## Arizona (AZ)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/az/
Last verified: 2026-05-07 (verified-2026)

Arizona offers Bilingual Education as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is an add-on endorsement. SEI training is mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 8.2% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-07.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses AZELLA (state-specific assessment).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2016.

Bilingual notes: Bilingual, PreK-12 endorsement under R7-2-615(J). Full endorsement = (a) approved bilingual program OR 21 semester hours of specified coursework, (b) 3-hr practicum OR 2 years bilingual classroom experience, (c) verified proficiency in a world language other than English (seven options: Arizona Classroom Spanish Proficiency Exam, AEPA/NES foreign-language portion, tribal verification of an American Indian language, comparable out-of-state exam, world-language degree, 3 years foreign-language teaching, or ACTFL OPI). Provisional endorsement (3 years, non-renewable) = prerequisite certificate + language-proficiency verification only.

ELD notes: English as a Second Language (ESL), PreK-12 endorsement under R7-2-615(K). Full endorsement = (a) approved ESL program OR 18 semester hours of specified coursework, (b) 3-hr ESL practicum OR 2 years ESL/bilingual experience, (c) a 'second language learning experience' (six-hour single-language coursework, intensive language training, third-semester placement, ACTFL OPI intermediate-low, AZ Spanish Proficiency Exam, American Indian language verification, or AEPA/NES foreign-language exam). The second-language requirement is exposure-not verified proficiency, hence languageProficiency=false. Provisional ESL = 6 hours of ESL coursework including methods (3 yrs, non-renewable). ADE explicitly states the ESL endorsement also authorizes teaching in a Structured English Immersion setting.

SEI notes: Universal mandate: per R7-2-615(L) and ADE OELAS, 'a Provisional or full SEI endorsement, or an ESL or Bilingual endorsement, shall be required of a teacher who is instructing students in a sheltered English immersion or structured English immersion model.' Originating in Proposition 203 (2000) and HB 2064 (2006), Arizona has the country's broadest teacher-of-EL credentialing mandate. The full SEI endorsement is earnable via 3 semester hours of approved coursework or 45 clock hours of approved professional development under A.R.S. § 15-756.09(B); the provisional version is 1 semester hour or 15 clock hours (3 years, non-renewable). Spring 2019 legislation reduced the daily SEI ELD block from 4 hours to 2 hours and re-opened broader access to dual-language and bilingual program models, but did not repeal the teacher endorsement mandate.

History:
- 1992-08-12: Flores v. Arizona filed (D. Ariz. CV-92-596-TUC-RCC) — Plaintiff parents in the Nogales Unified School District filed a class action alleging Arizona was violating the Equal Educational Opportunities Act of 1974 by underfunding programs for EL students. The case (later named Flores v. Arizona) drove the next two decades of EL policy in the state, leading to the 2000 district-court ruling that Arizona's per-pupil EL funding was "arbitrary and capricious" and forcing the legislature to act on EL teacher preparation and program funding. The case ultimately produced Horne v. Flores at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2009.
- 2000-11-07: Voters approve Proposition 203 (English for the Children) — Proposition 203 amends Arizona law to require Structured English Immersion as the default instructional model for ELs and lays the foundation for the universal SEI-endorsement mandate later codified in R7-2-615(L) and A.R.S. § 15-756.09.
- 2006-04-28: HB 2064 establishes SEI endorsement infrastructure — HB 2064 (50th Legislature, 2nd Regular Session) creates the Arizona English Language Learners Task Force and authorizes the SEI endorsement and SEI model — setting the 4-hour daily ELD block standard and embedding the SEI endorsement requirement for any teacher instructing ELs in an SEI setting.
- 2009-06-25: Horne v. Flores decided by U.S. Supreme Court (557 U.S. 433) — In a 5–4 decision, the U.S. Supreme Court vacated the lower courts' rulings against Arizona in the long-running Flores v. Arizona litigation and remanded for reconsideration in light of changed circumstances — namely Proposition 203's SEI mandate, HB 2064's new EL Task Force and SEI endorsement, and the federal No Child Left Behind framework. The decision narrowed the EEOA enforcement leverage federal courts had previously exercised over state EL programs and is the controlling SCOTUS precedent on EEOA "appropriate action" claims. The companion HB 2064 SEI infrastructure remained in force.
- 2016-05-12: Arizona Seal of Biliteracy authorized (SB 1239) — Governor signed SB 1239 (A.R.S. § 15-258) creating the Arizona State Seal of Biliteracy, recognizing high school graduates who attain proficiency in English and one or more world languages.
- 2019-07-09: HB 2435 reduces daily SEI/ELD block from 4 hours to 2 — Spring 2019 legislation (HB 2435, signed July 2019) reduced the mandatory daily SEI English Language Development block from 4 hours to 2 hours and re-opened access to dual-language and bilingual program models. The teacher-of-EL endorsement mandate under R7-2-615(L) was not repealed.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2026-05-07: Re-verified against current ADE sources — R7-2-615 re-read: bilingual.requirements.program null → true (R7-2-615(J)(4)(b) names an approved bilingual education program as Option A) and ELD.requirements.program null → true (R7-2-615(K)(3)(b) names an approved ESL program as Option A). Standards.el false → true — R7-2-602 Standard 2 explicitly references 'English language learners' and second-language acquisition. SEI mandate confirmed unchanged; notes expanded with Prop 203 (2000) / HB 2064 (2006) statutory backbone and the spring 2019 reduction of the daily SEI ELD block from 4 hours to 2 hours.

## Arkansas (AR)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/ar/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Arkansas does not offer a bilingual education credential; ELD/ESL is an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 8.1% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic.
- Uses ELPA21 (ELPA21 consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2018.

Bilingual notes: Arkansas does not offer a bilingual-education endorsement. Appendix A of the Rules Governing Educator Licensure (effective 2022-06-02) lists no bilingual credential. Foreign-language endorsements such as Spanish (code 710), French (248), and German (702) exist on the DESE licensure-area list but are world-language teaching credentials, not bilingual-program credentials.

ELD notes: Branded English as a Second Language (ESL, code 247) for the Standard License path and English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL, code 100) for the Ancillary License path; both are K-12 endorsements added to a primary teaching license. Per Rules §4-10.03.3 and §4-11.01, the endorsement is reachable by either an approved program of study (transcript pathway, internship 'if applicable') or by testing out — Appendix A Chart 1 marks ESOL (K-12) as available via both routes, and Chart 2 lists every first-time license level (B-K, K-6, 4-8, 4-12, 7-12, K-12, K-12 SpEd) as eligible to test out. Test-out instrument is the Praxis 5362 (English to Speakers of Other Languages), passing score 155 per the DESE Licensure Assessments page. State-prescribed competencies (Updated 2024 EEF document) cover five domains — Language, Culture, Planning/Implementing/Maintaining Instruction, Assessment, Professionalism — cross-walked to TESOL standards 1-5 and Praxis 5362 sections 1-6. No state-level minimum credit hours, clock hours, or practicum hours are published for the endorsement; approved programs set their own. No second-language proficiency requirement (ESOL is teaching English to non-English speakers, not bilingual instruction).

SEI notes: No statewide SEI / all-teacher EL training mandate. The current Rules Governing Educator Licensure contain no provisions requiring sheltered-instruction or EL coursework of teachers outside the ESOL endorsement; searches of the rules text for 'sheltered', 'SEI', 'all teachers', 'every teacher', and 'professional development' tied to English return no such mandate.

History:
- 2018-06-01: Arkansas Seal of Biliteracy adopted by State Board — Following a 2017-03 pilot launched by AFLTA and ARKTESOL, the Arkansas State Board of Education endorsed the Arkansas Seal of Biliteracy in June 2018, recognizing high school graduates who demonstrate proficiency in English plus one or more world languages.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2022-06-02: Rules Governing Educator Licensure (ADE 317-1) take effect — Updated Rules Governing Educator Licensure take effect, codifying the K-12 ESL endorsement (code 247) and K-12 ESOL Ancillary License (code 100) pathways with both approved-program and test-out (Praxis 5362, passing 155) routes per §4-10.03.3, §4-11.01, and Appendix A Charts 1-2.
- 2024-01-01: DESE refreshes ESL endorsement competencies and Arkansas Teaching Standards — DESE Educator Effectiveness Framework (EEF) republished the ESL K-12 Endorsement Competencies (TESOL- and Praxis-5362-aligned, five domains) and the Arkansas Teaching Standards (continuing to adopt the 2011 InTASC Model Core Teaching Standards as published, ten standards without expanded performance criteria).

## California (CA)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/ca/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

California offers Bilingual Education both as a standalone certification and as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 18.9% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ELPAC (state-specific assessment).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2011.

Bilingual notes: Bilingual Authorization (CL-628B) is the current new-issue add-on pathway (AB 1871, 2008); BCLAD/Bilingual Crosscultural Specialist Credential lineage is the standalone form. Pathways: (1) Commission-approved bilingual program; (2) CSET World Languages Tests II/III, IV, V; (3) program + CSET equivalency. Practicum not separately enumerated in leaflet — coded null.

ELD notes: EL Authorization / CLAD Certificate (CL-628C) plus embedded EL preparation in every Multiple/Single Subject preliminary credential issued since 7/1/2002 (AB 1059). Pathways include CTEL Examination, approved CTEL program, program+exam equivalency, legacy ESL/SDAIE, SB 1969/CCSD, NBPTS ENL, out-of-state equivalency. Second-language requirement waived for candidates with a bachelor's degree from a regionally-accredited institution.

SEI notes: California's SEI-equivalent mandate is the AB 1059 embedded EL authorization in every Multiple Subject and Single Subject preliminary credential issued since 7/1/2002 — functionally one-course-plus EL preparation required of every newly-credentialed classroom teacher.

History:
- 1976-09-21: Chacón-Moscone Bilingual-Bicultural Education Act enacted (AB 1329, Stats. 1976 ch. 978) — California's first comprehensive bilingual-education statute required districts to provide bilingual instruction wherever 10 or more EL students of the same primary language were enrolled in the same grade at a school. The act underwrote two decades of growth in California bilingual programs and bilingual-teacher credentialing infrastructure (the BCLAD pathway descends from it). The legislature allowed Chacón-Moscone to sunset in 1987, but the State Board of Education continued most of its requirements administratively until Proposition 227 (1998) overrode them.
- 1998-06-02: Voters approve Proposition 227 — English-only mandate (English in Public Schools Initiative) — Funded by Ron Unz, Prop 227 passed roughly 61%–39% and rewrote California Education Code §§300-340 to require Sheltered English Immersion for nearly all EL students, capping it at "normally not to exceed one year" and narrowing parental waivers. Bilingual programs collapsed statewide and the BCLAD credential pipeline contracted sharply. Prop 227 remained in force until voters approved Proposition 58 in 2016, which restored district choice. The Unz model exported to Arizona (Prop 203, 2000) and Massachusetts (Question 2, 2002).
- 2002-07-01: AB 1059 EL preparation embedded in every preliminary credential — Effective 2002-07-01 (AB 1059, 1999), every Multiple Subject and Single Subject preliminary teaching credential issued by California must embed EL preparation, making CA's universal EL-credentialing mandate functionally one-course-plus EL preparation required of every newly-credentialed classroom teacher.
- 2008-09-30: AB 1871 establishes current Bilingual Authorization (CL-628B) — AB 1871 (2008) restructured California's bilingual credentialing into the current Bilingual Authorization issued under CL-628B. Pathways: a Commission-approved bilingual program, CSET World Languages Tests II/III + IV + V, or program + CSET equivalency. Successor to the BCLAD/Bilingual Crosscultural Specialist Credential lineage.
- 2011-10-08: California State Seal of Biliteracy enacted (AB 815) — Governor signed AB 815 establishing the California State Seal of Biliteracy — the nation's first state-level Seal — recognizing high school graduates who attain proficiency in English and one or more world languages.
- 2016-11-08: Voters approve Proposition 58 (CA Ed.G.E. Act) — Proposition 58 (the California Education for a Global Economy Initiative) repeals the English-only instruction restrictions of Proposition 227 (1998), restoring local authority to offer bilingual, dual-language, and structured English immersion programs and reinforcing demand for the Bilingual Authorization.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2024-04-01: CTC adopts revised California Standards for the Teaching Profession (CSTP) — CTC adopted the April 2024 revision of the California Standards for the Teaching Profession; standards continue to reference EL/cultural/linguistic diversity explicitly and bind all California teachers.

## Colorado (CO)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/co/
Last verified: 2026-05-07 (verified-2026)

Colorado offers Bilingual Education as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 10.4% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-07.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2017.

Bilingual notes: Branded 'Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CLD) Bilingual Education' (Grades K-12). 'Added endorsement only' per CDE — applicants must first hold a Colorado initial or professional teacher license. Two pathways: (A) completion of a Colorado-State-Board-approved CLD Bilingual program (8.23), or (B) completion of the CLDE endorsement (8.22) coursework PLUS three CLD Bilingual competencies (Bilingualism and Biliteracy; Bilingual Methods, ≥15 clock hours; Ability to Teach in the Additional Language, ≥30 clock hours). Language proficiency in the partner language is required and is typically demonstrated via Praxis + ACTFL OPI in the chosen language or a degree in the language; the worksheet allows test scores OR equivalent coursework, so 'test' is coded null rather than true.

ELD notes: Branded 'Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CLD) Education' endorsement (Grades K-12). 'Added endorsement only.' Two pathways: (A) Colorado-State-Board-approved CLD program, or (B) 24 semester hours of coursework (B- or higher in each) across First/Second Language Acquisition, Literacy Development for CLD Students, Knowledge of English and Linguistics, Assessment of Language Proficiency, Foundations in CLD Education, Teaching Strategies for CLD Learners, CLD Field Experience (3 SH practicum), and Knowledge of Other Languages. Up to 6 of the 24 SH may come from documented professional development or work experience. No exam gate. The 'Knowledge of Other Languages' category does not require a language-proficiency exam — it can be satisfied by coursework, study abroad, a major/minor, or three additional hours in any other CLD category — so languageProficiency is coded false.

SEI notes: No general SEI mandate for all teachers. However, effective 2025-09-01, educators renewing a professional teaching license with an elementary, English language arts, math, science, or social studies endorsement must complete 45 clock hours (or 3 semester hours) of EL-focused professional learning aligned to the CLD standards. Holders of CLDE, CLD Bilingual, LDE, or LDE Bilingual endorsements are exempt. Districts with ≤2% EL enrollment over three years can request waivers. This is a renewal-gated PD rule for selected endorsements rather than a universal pre-service SEI mandate of the AZ/CA/MA type, so mandatedForAllTeachers remains false.

History:
- 1981-06-01: Colorado English Language Proficiency Act enacted (HB 1166) — The Colorado English Language Proficiency Act (ELPA), codified at C.R.S. §§ 22-24-101 to -106, established state funding for districts to provide language-acquisition services to EL students. Unlike the bilingual mandates in Massachusetts (1971), New Mexico (1973), or Illinois (1973), Colorado's ELPA is permissive in program model — districts may operate transitional bilingual, dual-language, or English-as-a-second-language programs — but it commits state funds (administered by CDE) to support whichever model the district chooses. ELPA remains the funding backbone for Colorado EL services and underpins the modern CLDE office at CDE.
- 2002-11-05: Voters reject Amendment 31 — Colorado declines to adopt an English-only mandate — Funded by Ron Unz, Amendment 31 sought to replicate California's Proposition 227 (1998) and Arizona's Proposition 203 (2000) by requiring Sheltered English Immersion in Colorado public schools. Voters defeated it roughly 56%–44%, the first state-level rejection of the Unz English-only model. The vote preserved Colorado's permissive English Language Proficiency Act framework and is why Colorado today has no statutory SEI mandate (the comparable column on the map for CO codes false), in contrast to its three immediate neighbors that adopted the model.
- 2012-07-01: Colorado joins WIDA Consortium — Colorado joined the WIDA Consortium in 2012 and adopted ACCESS for ELLs as the state's annual English language proficiency assessment, replacing legacy state-specific instruments.
- 2017-04-04: Diploma Endorsement for Biliteracy enacted (SB17-123) — Governor signed SB17-123 establishing Colorado's High School Diploma Endorsement for Biliteracy (Seal of Biliteracy), recognizing graduates proficient in English and one or more world languages.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2025-09-01: 45-hour EL professional-development requirement takes effect — Effective 2025-09-01, educators renewing a Colorado professional teaching license with an elementary, ELA, math, science, or social-studies endorsement must complete 45 clock hours (or 3 semester hours) of EL-focused professional learning aligned to the CLD standards. CLDE / CLD Bilingual / LDE / LDE Bilingual endorsement holders are exempt; districts at ≤2% EL enrollment over three years can request waivers.
- 2026-05-07: Re-verified against current CDE sources — Bilingual reclassified standalone → add-on (CDE explicitly classifies both CLDE and CLD Bilingual Education as 'added endorsements only'). New 45-hour EL professional-development requirement effective 2025-09-01 for educators renewing licenses with elementary, ELA, math, science, or social-studies endorsements. Standards corrections: linguistic true → false (text says 'language', not 'linguistic'); el false → true (2011 Quality Standards 2.4 explicitly names English language learners).

## Connecticut (CT)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/ct/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Connecticut offers Bilingual Education as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 9.4% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, el.
- Uses LAS Links Online (state-specific assessment).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2017.

Bilingual notes: CT issues bilingual qualifications as cross-endorsements (no standalone bilingual license). Requires 18 semester hours across six areas at one regionally accredited college, plus ACTFL OPI + WPT in the target language and Praxis Core writing in English. Most bilingual endorsements layer on top of an existing primary endorsement; secondary bilingual humanities (#991) and STEM (#992) are exceptions requiring 15 content-area hours instead. ARCTEL exists as an alternate program-based pathway, hence program=null rather than false. Baseline-2019 coded offered=false; this refresh corrects to offered=true,addOn=true.

ELD notes: CT offers BOTH the Initial TESOL Teaching Certificate (PK-12, standalone) and a TESOL cross-endorsement. Standalone pathway requires an approved preparation program with TESOL student teaching and Praxis II ESOL. Cross-endorsement requires 30 semester hours of TESOL coursework across five categories (English Syntax/Composition; Language Theory; Linguistic and Academic Assessment of ELLs; Curriculum and Methods of Teaching ESL; Culture and Intergroup Relations). Schema fields are coded on the strength of the standalone pathway.

SEI notes: No statewide SEI mandate. Connecticut General Statutes §10-17f triggers bilingual programs when a school enrolls 20+ ELs of the same language background; ESL/sheltered instruction elsewhere is delivered by TESOL-credentialed teachers. Statewide SEI mandates exist in MA/AZ/CA (and phasing in NV) but not CT.

History:
- 1977-06-08: Connecticut Bilingual Education Act enacted (Public Act 77-588) — Public Act 77-588 (codified at C.G.S. § 10-17f et seq.) required Connecticut school districts with 20 or more EL students of the same dominant language at any one school to provide a bilingual education program. The 1977 act was substantially amended in 1999 (Public Act 99-211) to cap bilingual program participation at 30 months per student, and again in 2017 (Public Act 17-173) to extend the cap by an additional 30 months under specified conditions. The §10-17f trigger threshold is the current statutory backbone for CT's bilingual cross-endorsement framework.
- 2017-06-06: Connecticut State Seal of Biliteracy enacted (Public Act 17-29) — Governor signed Public Act 17-29 establishing the Connecticut State Seal of Biliteracy, recognizing high school graduates who attain proficiency in English plus one or more world languages. SDE administers the Seal in partnership with districts.
- 2017-07-01: CSDE adopts CCT Rubric for Effective Teaching (2017 edition) — CSDE released the 2017 edition of the Common Core of Teaching (CCT) Rubric for Effective Teaching, the foundational professional-standards document binding all CT teachers. Keyword scan: 'diverse', 'cultural', and 'English learner' present; 'linguistic' absent — driving professionalStandardsMentions.linguistic = false.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2026-05-08: Bilingual cross-endorsement scope corrected on refresh — Re-verification against current CSDE certification pages corrected the baseline coding of bilingual.offered from false to true (CT issues bilingual qualifications as cross-endorsements under an 18 semester-hour framework with ACTFL OPI/WPT and Praxis Core writing). No CSDE policy changed; the diff is a baseline-2019 miscoding fix.

## District of Columbia (DC)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/dc/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

District of Columbia offers Bilingual Education both as a standalone certification and as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. ELD notes: DC's canonical SEA term is 'English as a Second Language' (ESL). Praxis 5362 (English to Speakers of Other Languages, score 155) is the required content exam, with PLT or World Languages Pedagogy as the pedagogy exam.

SEI notes: DC recognizes five EL program models for LEAs (dual language, inclusion/collaborative, content-based ESL, sheltered content, newcomer) but does not mandate sheltered English instruction training for all teachers.

History:
- 2014-12-04: DC adopts the State Seal of Biliteracy — The DC State Board of Education and OSSE established a Seal of Biliteracy for high-school graduates demonstrating proficiency in English plus one or more additional world languages, making DC one of the earliest adopters in the country.

For ESL it specifies Praxis 5362 (English to Speakers of Other Languages, score 155) plus PLT or World Languages Pedagogy; for Bilingual Education it requires a completed degree major or completion of an approved program plus a PLT pedagogy exam, with no Praxis content exam and no language-proficiency exam listed.

## Florida (FL)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/fl/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Florida does not offer a bilingual education credential; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 9.5% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2016.

Bilingual notes: Florida has no separate bilingual education certification or endorsement. Bilingual program delivery is staffed by ESOL-credentialed teachers, often paired with a World Language certification (e.g., Spanish K-12) where appropriate.

ELD notes: Florida offers two ESOL credentials: (1) the standalone ESOL K-12 certification under Rule 6A-4.0245 (FTCE 047 ESOL K-12 subject area exam, or major in ESOL); and (2) the ESOL academic endorsement under Rule 6A-4.0244, which requires 15 semester hours across five areas (Methods, Curriculum and Materials, Cross-Cultural Communication, Applied Linguistics, Testing and Evaluation) — or a Florida district's approved inservice add-on program. The State Board adopted new ESOL endorsement standards on 2025-08-20 under Rule 6A-4.02451 (effective Sep 2025); approved programs must submit revised matrices to FLDOE by 2026-06-01. No language-proficiency exam (LOTE) is required.

SEI notes: Florida operates under the LULAC v. State Board of Education Consent Decree (1990-08-14), which mandates ESOL training scaled by teacher category: Category I (Language Arts/English/Reading/Elementary/ESE serving ELLs) needs the full ESOL endorsement (15 SH or 300 inservice points) or FTCE 047 plus 2 ESOL courses; Category II (math/science/social studies/computer literacy) needs 1 course or 60 inservice points; Category III (fine arts/electives, SLPs, OT/PT) needs 1 course or 18 inservice points; Category IV (school-based administrators and counselors) needs 1 course. Training is conditional on serving ELLs in covered roles, so this is not equivalent to the AZ/CA/MA model where SEI is mandated for all teachers regardless of student population.

History:
- 1990-08-14: LULAC v. State Board of Education Consent Decree entered — The federal consent decree settling LULAC v. SBE established Florida's framework for serving ELs and trained teachers, including the category-conditional ESOL training requirements (Categories I–IV) that remain the operative SEI-style mandate in Florida. The decree is the foundation for Rules 6A-4.0244 (endorsement) and 6A-4.0245 (standalone K-12 certification).
- 2016-04-14: Florida adopts the State Seal of Biliteracy — Florida Statute § 1003.432 (HB 7029, 2016) authorizes a Gold and Silver Seal of Biliteracy on the high-school diploma for graduates demonstrating proficiency in English plus one or more world languages.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2025-08-20: State Board adopts 2025 Florida Teacher Standards for ESOL Endorsement — The State Board adopted Rule 6A-4.02451 establishing new ESOL endorsement standards (effective September 2025), replacing the 2010 standards. The five-strand structure (Culture, Applied Linguistics, Methods of Teaching, Curriculum and Materials, Testing and Evaluation) is preserved; approved programs must submit revised matrices to FLDOE by 2026-06-01.
- 2026-05-08: Refreshed against current SEA sources (verified-2026) — Re-verified Rules 6A-4.0244 and 6A-4.0245, the Consent Decree page, the 2025 ESOL endorsement standards, FEAP (6A-5.065), and FTCE 047. Updated elPercent to 9.5% (NCES Fall 2021) and set eld.requirements.coursework=true to reflect the rule-mandated 15 SH across five areas.

## Hawaii (HI)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/hi/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Hawaii offers a standalone Bilingual Education certification; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 10.0% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2015.

Bilingual notes: HTSB issues standalone 'Kaiapuni Hawaiʻi / Hawaiian Language Immersion' and 'ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi / Hawaiian Language' license fields, which roll up under the canonical 'bilingual' umbrella as heritage/medium-of-instruction credentials. These primarily serve Native Hawaiian / Hawaiian-medium students rather than classified ELs in the Spanish/Asian-language sense; requirements are null pending direct citation of HTSB rules (HAR 8-54 series), which were not reachable from this verification session.

ELD notes: HTSB issues a standalone 'Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages' (TESOL) license field at P-3, K-6, 6-8, 6-12, P-12, and K-12 grade bands. Coursework and a content test are required (Praxis ESOL); program and practicum requirements are null because HTSB's content-area-specific rules pages were not reachable from this 2026 refresh session.

History:
- 1978-11-07: Hawaii Constitution amended — Hawaiian becomes co-official language with English — At the 1978 Constitutional Convention voters ratified Article XV § 4 of the Hawaii State Constitution, making Hawaiian (ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi) an official language of the State alongside English — the only U.S. state to officially recognize a Native language at constitutional level. Article X § 4 simultaneously requires the State to promote "the study of Hawaiian culture, history, and language." The 1978 amendments are the constitutional predicate for the Hawaiian-medium (Kaiapuni) public-school program, the HTSB Hawaiian Language Immersion teacher fields that this record codes under bilingual, and the State's bilingual approach to EL students whose home language is Hawaiian or a Pacific-Island language.
- 1986-06-16: Act 89 lifts the ban on Hawaiian-medium public instruction — The Hawaii Legislature passed Act 89 (1986) repealing the lingering 1896 prohibition on teaching public school subjects in Hawaiian. Coupled with the 1978 constitutional amendment, Act 89 enabled the Department of Education to establish Ka Papahana Kaiapuni — the Hawaiian-medium public-school program — initially at two pilot sites in 1987 and now at over 20 schools statewide. Act 89 is the operational basis for the Hawaiian Language Immersion teacher fields HTSB issues today and is functionally why Hawaii is coded as a bilingual-program-offering state.
- 2015-07-14: Hawaii adopts the State Seal of Biliteracy — Act 224 (SLH 2015 / SB 1394) authorizes a State Seal of Biliteracy for graduating high-school students who demonstrate proficiency in English plus one or more additional languages, including ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi. Hawaii is among the early-adopter states.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2021-10-01: NCES Fall 2021 EL count: 17,353 students (10.0%) — Per NCES Digest Table 204.20, Hawaii's classified-EL share of public-school enrollment rose to 10.0% in Fall 2021, up from 9.5% in Fall 2020 and 7.0% at its 2016 trough. The state remains a WIDA Consortium member and administers ACCESS for ELLs annually.
- 2026-05-08: Refreshed against current SEA sources (verified-2026) — Re-verified HTSB license fields (TESOL + Hawaiian-medium fields), Hawaii Teacher Performance Standards, and NCES EL counts. Re-coded bilingual.offered to true to reflect HTSB's standalone Hawaiian Language Immersion / ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi fields, which roll up under the canonical bilingual umbrella as heritage/medium-of-instruction credentials. ELD requirements left partially null where HTSB's content-area rule pages were not reachable.

## Idaho (ID)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/id/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Idaho offers Bilingual Education both as a standalone certification and as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 5.8% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2020.

Bilingual notes: Bilingual Education (K-12) endorsement (code 7038). Issued via SBOE-approved EPP program (e.g., BSU, NNU) per the OSBE-approved endorsement programs matrix. IDAPA 08.02.02 §021 requires credit hours + a state-board-approved content/pedagogy/performance assessment + supervised clinical experience for any standard endorsement; the Institutional Recommendation form (Jan 2025) requires a Praxis content assessment per endorsement. Idaho Standards for Bilingual Education Teachers (in the 2018 Standards for Initial Certification doc, still operative for this discipline) Standard 4(a) requires program-verified L1 and L2 academic language proficiency.

ELD notes: English as a Second Language (ESL) (K-12) endorsement (code 7126). The SDE *English Learner Program Manual* (2025) uses the term 'English as a New Language (ENL)' for the corresponding teaching assignment codes; both names refer to the same 7126 endorsement. Same IDAPA 08.02.02 §021 requirements (coursework + content assessment + supervised clinical experience) apply.

SEI notes: No Idaho statute or SBOE rule mandates that all certified teachers obtain an EL/SEI endorsement. ESL/ENL and Bilingual remain voluntary specializations. The SDE EL Program Manual (2025) recommends professional development for all language and content teachers but does not impose an SEA-level mandate.

History:
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2020-03-23: Idaho adopts the State Seal of Biliteracy — House Bill 433 (2020) authorized the Idaho Seal of Biliteracy on the high-school diploma for graduates demonstrating proficiency in English plus one or more world languages, administered through the Idaho SDE.
- 2022-07-01: Idaho updates Standards for Initial Certification (program-approval date) — The 2024 edition of the *Idaho Standards for Initial Certification of Professional School Personnel* (program-approval date July 1, 2022) updates the Idaho Core Teaching Standards and adds Comprehensive Literacy Standards. The 2018 edition's discipline standards for Bilingual Education and ESL teachers remain operative for those endorsements.
- 2025-08-01: SDE issues updated English Learner Program Manual — Idaho SDE published the 08/01/2025 update of the *English Learner Program Manual*. The 'Idaho ESL and Bilingual Teacher Certification' assignment-code table (pp. 40–42) confirms Bilingual (K-12) endorsement code 7038 and ESL/ENL (K-12) code 7126, and confirms Idaho's WIDA Consortium membership (ACCESS for ELLs / WIDA Screener).
- 2026-05-08: Refreshed against current SEA sources (verified-2026) — Re-verified IDAPA 08.02.02 §017/§021, the OSBE-approved EPP endorsement matrix, the 2018 and 2024 initial-certification standards, the 2025 EL Program Manual, the SDE Institutional Recommendation form, and NCES counts. ## Illinois (IL)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/il/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Illinois offers Bilingual Education both as a standalone certification and as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 12.8% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2013.

ELD notes: Distinguishes ENL (English-only) from ESL (allows native-language support). 18 SH coursework + 100-hr practicum required for the subsequent endorsement.

SEI notes: No SEI mandate. District-level TBE/TPI required under 105 ILCS 5/14C and 23 IAC 228 — TBE for attendance centers with 20+ same-language ELs, TPI for fewer. 23 IAC 24.140 takes effect 2026-07-01 and drops explicit ELL language from the IPTS; flag for next refresh.

History:
- 1973-08-21: Illinois Transitional Bilingual Education Act enacted (PA 78-727) — Public Act 78-727 created Article 14C of the Illinois School Code (105 ILCS 5/14C), one of the strongest state TBE mandates in the country. Article 14C requires any public school attendance center with 20 or more EL students of the same language background to operate a Transitional Bilingual Education program for at least three years per student, and any school with fewer than 20 to provide a Transitional Program of Instruction (TPI) — i.e., ESL-based services. The 1973 statute is the legal source of Illinois's bilingual-and-ESL endorsement structure and of the state's bilingual-teacher Type-29 credential lineage that 23 IAC Part 25 later modernized. Illinois followed Massachusetts (1971), New Mexico (1973), and Texas (1973) in mandating bilingual instruction by statute.
- 2013-08-23: Illinois adopts State Seal of Biliteracy (PA 098-0560) — Illinois became one of the first states to authorize a State Seal of Biliteracy on high-school diplomas, certifying graduates' proficiency in English and one or more world languages. ISBE administers the program with district-level participation; the affordance is now embedded in graduation pathways and feeds into the Bilingual/ESL teacher pipeline.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2026-05-08: Re-audit (history events captured) — Re-audited current sources and confirmed all coding still grounded. No substantive coding changes from the 2026-05-08 verification; this pass added missing history rows (Seal of Biliteracy authorization; IPTS 24.140 phase-in) per the §3a history-capture emphasis.
- 2026-07-01: 23 IAC 24.140 supersedes 24.130 as Illinois Professional Teaching Standards — ISBE's revised Illinois Professional Teaching Standards (23 IAC 24.140) take effect 2026-07-01, replacing 23 IAC 24.130. The new standards drop the explicit 'English language learners' phrasing that 24.130 carried, shifting EL-relevant competencies under broader 'diverse learners' language. Flag for re-coding `professionalStandardsMentions.el` after the transition.

## Indiana (IN)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/in/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Indiana does not offer a bilingual education credential; ELD/ESL is available both as a standalone license and as an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 7.0% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2015.

Bilingual notes: IDOE does not issue a bilingual / dual language teaching credential. World-language licenses (Spanish, French, German, Chinese, etc.) authorize the language as a content area but do not authorize content-area instruction in that language.

ELD notes: The English as a New Language (ENL) Professional Educator License is the EL credential. It is issued via (a) completion of an IDOE-approved educator preparation program at a regionally-accredited university, plus (b) passage of a state-approved content exam — Indiana CORE 019 'English Learners' or Praxis 5362 'English to Speakers of Other Languages' (cut score 155). Both Indiana CORE and Praxis tables flag ENL as 'No — must complete approved educator preparation program', so test alone is not sufficient. Coursework is part of the approved program (varies by university; IDOE does not enumerate uniform credit hours). The temporary EL Teacher of Record (ToR) Rubric — an alternate path for already-licensed teachers based on SLA coursework, EL teaching years, and PD points — closed to new candidates on September 1, 2022. After that date, the only options to serve as an EL ToR are full ENL licensure or an ENL Emergency Permit (one-year, LEA-issued, requires demonstrated progress toward full licensure to renew). Practicum is set at the program/institution level rather than by a uniform IDOE rule, so the field is null. No partner-language proficiency exam is required (ENL is not a bilingual credential).

SEI notes: There is no universal SEI / EL coursework mandate on all Indiana teachers. The federal-compliance structure IDOE imposes is per-LEA: every LEA must designate at least one qualified 'EL Teacher of Record' (ENL-licensed or ENL Emergency Permit holder) for its EL students. Non-ENL-licensed classroom teachers may serve ELs as a 'Teacher of Service' (ToS) under ToR oversight, with ongoing job-embedded EL training, but this does not require all teachers to obtain ENL coursework.

History:
- 2015-04-30: Indiana adopts Indiana Seal of Biliteracy — Indiana enacted its Seal of Biliteracy program (HEA 1638), recognizing graduates proficient in English plus one or more additional languages. IDOE administers the credential at the district level; participation has expanded steadily since adoption.
- 2019-08-09: IDOE issues EL Program Staffing memo defining 'EL Teacher of Record' — IDOE clarified that every LEA serving ELs must designate at least one ENL-licensed (or ENL Emergency Permit) EL Teacher of Record. Non-ENL classroom teachers may serve ELs as Teachers of Service under ToR oversight. This memo is the operative staffing rule that replaces a generic SEI mandate in Indiana.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2022-09-01: EL ToR alternate qualification path closes — The alternate-qualification rubric path that allowed non-ENL-licensed teachers to be qualified as EL Teacher of Record sunset on 2022-09-01. ENL licensure (or an ENL Emergency Permit) is now the sole pathway to ToR status, tightening the credential market for EL services.
- 2026-05-08: Re-audit (history events captured) — Re-audited against current IDOE sources. No coding changes; this pass added Seal of Biliteracy adoption, EL Program Staffing memo, and EL ToR alternate-path sunset to the history log per the §3a history-capture emphasis.

## Kansas (KS)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/ks/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Kansas does not offer a bilingual education credential; ELD/ESL is an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 8.0% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic, el.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2016.

Bilingual notes: Kansas does not offer a bilingual-education teacher credential. Neither the KSDE 'Adding an Endorsement' page nor the Higher Education Teacher Preparation Standards index lists a bilingual endorsement; only an ESOL endorsement exists.

ELD notes: ESOL endorsement (K.A.R. 91-1-203, updated March 2023) is an add-on to an existing Kansas teaching license, with two pathways: Option 1 — complete a state-approved ESOL program at a Kansas IHE plus pass the state-approved ESOL content exam; Option 2 ('Test Plus') — complete state-approved ESOL content-specific coursework at an approved KS institution (e.g., FHSU ESOL 884/885; KU C&T 330/331/491 or 820/825; K-State EDCI 420/431 or 720/742; McPherson CI 428/628; Newman EDUC 6133/6113; Washburn ED 650/624; Wichita State CI 775) plus pass the ESOL content exam. Practicum is included in some institutional pathways (FHSU, KU) but is not a statewide regulatory requirement, so coded null.

SEI notes: Kansas has no statewide sheltered-English-instruction (SEI) mandate for all teachers. The Professional Education Standards (adopted 2015, revised 2016) embed EL-relevant competencies in Standard 2 (Learning Differences) — including 2.1.5PS on strategies for making content accessible to English language learners — but these are teacher-preparation program standards, not an SEI endorsement requirement.

History:
- 2015-01-13: Kansas adopts revised Professional Education Teacher Preparation Standards — KSBE adopted Kansas's current Professional Education Teacher Preparation Standards on 2015-01-13. Standard 2 (Learning Differences) embeds EL-relevant competencies (e.g., 2.1.5PS — strategies for making content accessible to English language learners) into the general preparation framework that binds all Kansas-prepared teachers.
- 2016-04-29: Professional Education Standards updated to add ESOL/virtual-learning content — KSBE edited the Professional Education Teacher Preparation Standards on 2016-04-29 to make ESOL and virtual-learning competencies explicit within the general preparation document. This is the textual basis for `professionalStandardsMentions.el = true` on Kansas's record.
- 2016-05-10: Kansas adopts State Seal of Biliteracy — Kansas formally adopted a State Seal of Biliteracy program in 2016, recognizing high-school graduates proficient in English plus one or more world languages. KSDE publishes program guidance; participation is district-opt-in.
- 2017-05-09: KSBE adopts ESOL Teacher Preparation Standards — Kansas adopted the standalone ESOL (K-6, 5-8, 6-12, PreK-12) Teacher Preparation Standards on 2017-05-09. These define the competency floor for the ESOL endorsement (the only EL credential offered in Kansas, as an add-on to a primary license).
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2026-05-08: Re-audit (history events captured) — Re-audited against current KSDE sources. No coding changes; this pass added Professional Education standards adoption, the 2016 ESOL revision, Seal of Biliteracy adoption, and ESOL standards adoption to the history log per the §3a history-capture emphasis.

## Louisiana (LA)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/la/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Louisiana offers Bilingual Education as an add-on endorsement; ELD/ESL is an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 4.9% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards do not explicitly reference any of: diverse, cultural, linguistic, or English learner.
- Uses ELPT (state-specific assessment).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2014.

Bilingual notes: Bulletin 746 (Title 28, Part CXXXI) §1343 Bilingual Specialist add-on. Available to elementary, secondary, or all-level certified foreign-language teachers; requires 6 semester hours (Bilingual Methods I and II). languageProficiency=true reflects the prerequisite that the candidate already hold a Louisiana foreign-language certification, which functions as a target-language proficiency gate. baseline-2019 coded bilingual.offered=false; the 2019 paper appears to have missed this small endorsement.

ELD notes: Bulletin 746 §1359 English as a Second Language add-on. 12 semester hours / four 3-hour courses (Methods of Teaching ESL; Introduction to Language and Culture; Structure of the English Language; Curriculum Design for the Multicultural Classroom) on top of a valid OS, Type A/B/C, or Level 1/2/3 teaching certificate. No required exam, no separate practicum, no language-proficiency exam. program=null because the regulation prescribes coursework rather than a state-approved EPP pathway distinct from it.

SEI notes: Structured English Immersion is one of several program models LEAs may operate (per the EL Program Handbook), not a statewide pre-certification training mandate. Bulletin 746 imposes no SEI training requirement on general-certification candidates.

History:
- 1968-07-20: Act 409 creates CODOFIL and authorizes French-language public-school instruction — Act 409 of the 1968 Louisiana Legislature established the Council for the Development of French in Louisiana (CODOFIL) and directed BESE to take whatever steps are necessary to encourage the teaching of French in the public schools, formally reversing decades of post-1916 English-only state policy that had suppressed Cajun and Creole French. CODOFIL's reciprocal teacher-recruitment programs with France, Belgium, and Quebec became the operational model for Louisiana French immersion programs (now ~30+ schools statewide), and Act 409 is the legal predicate for the BESE-approved French-immersion bilingual programs that Louisiana operates alongside its newer Spanish-immersion strands. The 1974 Louisiana Constitution (Article XII §4) further commits the State to preserve, foster, and promote its linguistic origins.
- 2014-05-16: Louisiana adopts State Seal of Biliteracy — Louisiana adopted the State Seal of Biliteracy on 2014-05-16, recognizing high-school graduates proficient in English plus one or more world languages. LDOE administers the program with district-level participation.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2023-08-01: BESE Bulletin 746 ESL/Bilingual add-on rule revised (emergency rule) — BESE issued an August 2023 emergency rule updating Bulletin 746 §1359 (ESL add-on) and §1343 (Bilingual Specialist add-on) certification requirements. LDOE's published applicant checklists track the revised rule. This is the operative pathway document for ESL/Bilingual add-on candidates today.
- 2024-04-01: Louisiana Educator Rubric (LEADS) released; statewide rollout 2025-26 — LDOE published the Louisiana Educator Rubric (LEADS) in April 2024 as the successor to the Compass Teacher Rubric, with statewide rollout in 2025-26. The rubric carries the state's professional-practice expectations for all teachers and is the document examined for `professionalStandardsMentions`.
- 2026-05-08: Re-audit (history events captured) — Re-audited against current LDOE/BESE sources. No coding changes; this pass added Seal of Biliteracy adoption, the 2023 Bulletin 746 emergency rule, and the LEADS rubric release to the history log per the §3a history-capture emphasis.

## Maine (ME)

URL: https://projectcert.org/states/me/
Last verified: 2026-05-08 (verified-2026)

Maine does not offer a bilingual education credential; ELD/ESL is an add-on endorsement. SEI training is not mandated for all teachers. As of 2021, 3.1% of public-school students are classified English Learners (NCES). Re-verified against current SEA sources on 2026-05-08.

- Professional teaching standards explicitly reference: diverse, cultural, linguistic.
- Uses ACCESS for ELLs (WIDA Consortium member).
- Seal of Biliteracy adopted in 2018.

ELD notes: Endorsement 660 (ESOL) under Chapter 115 Part II §1.8. Pathway 1 = approved Maine ESOL preparation program; Pathway 3 = 24 SH coursework + one academic semester (≥15 weeks) student teaching; Pathway 5 = approved portfolio. The 5/14/2025 amendment dropped the conditional-cert and Pathway 2 floors from 24 to 15 SH. requirements.test is null because Chapter 115 Part II does not name a Praxis content test for 660; third-party sites cite Praxis 5362 but the binding rule does not.

SEI notes: Sheltered instruction is one optional service component per the 10/9/2025 administrative letter and multilingual-services staffing guidance, not a statewide mandate.

History:
- 2018-10-31: Maine adopts Seal of Biliteracy — Maine joined the Seal of Biliteracy program in October 2018, recognizing high school graduates who demonstrate proficiency in English and one or more world languages. Administered through the Maine DOE.
- 2019-12-01: Baseline coding (Leider, Colombo & Nerlino, 2021) — Initial coding of the SEA's bilingual, ELD/ESL, and SEI credentials, professional teaching standards, and EL-population data. Captured Oct–Dec 2019 for the EPAA 29(100) document analysis; this row is the as-of-2019 snapshot against which subsequent verifications are diffed.
- 2025-05-14: Chapter 115 Part II amended; ESOL coursework floor reduced 24 → 15 SH — The 5/14/2025 amendment to Chapter 115 Part II §1.8 reduced the conditional-certificate floor and Pathway 2 floor for the 660 (ESOL) endorsement from 24 to 15 semester hours. Pathway 3 retains its 24 SH and one-semester student-teaching requirement. The amendment did not introduce a state-named Praxis content test for the endorsement.
- 2025-10-09: DOE administrative letter on multilingual-services staffing — Maine DOE issued an administrative letter and accompanying staffing guidance clarifying that sheltered instruction is one optional component of a district's multilingual-learner service model rather than a statewide mandate for all teachers. Confirms the schema's `sei.mandatedForAllTeachers: false` coding.

The teacher-candidate language requirement is unusual nationally.
